newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-MARLINS LAND LEYLAND AS NEW MANAGER.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-MARLINS LAND LEYLAND AS NEW MANAGER.

text.p: The Florida Marlins won the Jim Leyland sweepstakes on Friday, announcing they had signed the former Pittsburgh Pirates skipper to a five-year contract.
Terms of the contract were not announced but it has been reported that an estimated $7 million deal ended a bidding war for Leyland.
The California Angels, Chicago White Sox and Boston Red Sox were all vying for the services of Leyland, who decided to leave the cost-conscious Pirates at the end of this season.
"I made this decision based on heart. It was not a financial decision," Leyland told a news conference at Pro Player Stadium.
He called on the team, its management and fans to unite in an effort to overtake the powerhouse Atlanta Braves in the National League East.
"This is a great challenge for us. But we can only do it as a team," he said. "There can only be one heartbeat here from this day on."
The signing of Leyland was another coup for Marlins owner Wayne Huizenga, who also landed highly-prized NFL coach Jimmy Johnson to run his Miami Dolphins this year.
"This is one of the biggest days in the history of the Florida Marlins," said General Manager Dave Dombrosky.
The Marlins fired manager Rene Lachemann in July and named John Boles as the second manager in the club's history. Florida was 40-35 under Boles and finished 80-82 overall.

Leyland, a former manager of the year, led the Pirates to three consecutive National League East titles from 1990 to 1992, but he became frustrated by management cost-cutting in recent years, which saw the departure of such established stars as Bobby Bonilla, Barry Bonds and Doug Drabek.
The final straw may have come when the Pirates traded ace left-hander Denny Neagle in August to pitching-rich Atlanta in exchange for more young prospects.

The Pirates finished in last-place in the Central Division with a 73-89 record this season. During the 1996 campaign, the Pirates used 21 pitchers, many of them rookies whom Leyland said were not ready to pitch in the major leagues.
The 51-year-old Leyland had managed the Pirates since 1986, posting an 849-860 record in 11 years.
But he decided he had to make a move to a team with an owner willing to spend money on talent for a legitimate run at a championship.
"I like what I see," Leyland said of his new club. "The Marlins are moving in the right direction."
